title: Faustina Kowalska (1905–1938)
hookLine: a Polish sister records a message of mercy: Jesus, I trust in you

lines: TWO RAYS, ONE PALE, ONE RED.
cards: A painter's studio in Vilnius. A priest has hired an artist to paint a picture to a nun's description. She comes in to check on it.
Jesus in a white robe, one hand raised in blessing, the other touching his chest, where two rays stream out, one pale and one red.
The nun looks at the canvas, and, by her own account in her diary, she goes away and weeps, because it isn't as beautiful as what she saw. Her name is Sister Faustina Kowalska.

teach.b: First, the ordinary work. She came from a poor farming family in Poland, worked as a housekeeper, then joined a congregation of sisters. There she did the plain jobs: cook, gardener, the sister at the gate.
She wrote that Jesus spoke to her about his mercy, asked for the image to be painted, and asked that it carry a signature: Jesus, I trust in you.
At her confessor's request, she wrote down what she experienced in a diary, which became a long book. Third, the chaplet.
She recorded a short prayer, prayed on ordinary rosary beads, that keeps asking for mercy on us and on the whole world. It takes a few minutes.
Catholics pray it at home, in hospitals, and at three in the afternoon, the hour tradition links to Jesus's death. Fourth, the old word. Divine Mercy was not a new idea.
Psalm one hundred thirty-five, in the Douay-Rheims, repeats one refrain over and over: "for his mercy endureth for ever."

Faustina's message sends people back to that refrain, with a name and a face attached, and asks for one thing in return: trust. Not trust that life will go smoothly. Faustina was ill for years and died young.

Trust, as she wrote of it, that mercy is bigger than anything a person has done. The Church later canonized her, and her image now hangs in churches far from Poland, the rays still pale and red, the line still underneath.

how: Catholics who keep this devotion pray the Divine Mercy chaplet on rosary beads, often at three in the afternoon, and the image with its signature 'Jesus, I trust in you' hangs in parish churches; the Sunday after Easter is kept as Divine Mercy Sunday.

s: Faustina painted the Divine Mercy image herself
an artist painted it to her description, and she wept that it wasn't as beautiful as what she saw.
in her convent she did plain jobs like cooking and gardening
cook, gardener, and the sister at the gate.
Divine Mercy was a brand-new idea
the Psalm repeats it: his mercy endureth for ever.

games.q: you're Faustina. you've described an image, and a painter has finished it. it's not as beautiful as what you saw. what do you do?
games.why: by her own account she wept. the image was kept, and it still carries the line: Jesus, I trust in you.

practice: If you pray, take rosary beads or use your fingers, and on each bead ask for mercy on yourself and on the whole world, in the chaplet's words or your own; the whole chaplet runs longer than this, so simply begin.
If you don't pray, let one face come to mind, someone you find hard to forgive, and hold it a moment without judging it. Then rest.

wordCard.voice: Divine Mercy. God's mercy, as Saint Faustina's diary and image present it, summed up in five words: Jesus, I trust in you.

orig.note: Polish: Jesus, I trust in you, the signature on the image, in Faustina's own language.
